name: Grace Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six and catch two buses to campus for anatomy, chemistry and the skills lab, then eat a sandwich in the library. At weekends I work as a care assistant at Elmwood, a care home ten minutes from my mum's flat, doing breakfasts and helping residents wash. I'm tired by Sunday night, but the skills lab, where we practise turning a patient on a dummy, makes it feel real. I won a scholarship place for nursing, so I can't afford to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because nursing is about people, and a computer can't turn a patient or hold a hand. Maybe it saves a few minutes on charting. My real fight is staffing, not software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'm not relaxed, because plateau means the same old pressures. The loan is still there, and Elmwood already cuts staff. I'd still have a job at the end, so that part is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekend shifts, apply for the hospital bursary in second year and stay on the same two buses. I'd go to the student nurses' union meetings too. I wouldn't touch AI, since there's no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but tired. I feel fine about the nursing itself, and it's the money part that makes my stomach go tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money talk makes your stomach tight. What number do you carry in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty thousand of loan is a number I do on the bus, and my mum's agency pay hasn't moved in four years. If a hospital pays properly I'll be fine, but I won't know until I'm there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the staffing at Elmwood?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners of Elmwood, a chain based somewhere far away, and the government that lets them. They cut two carers per shift and call it efficiency. I'd rather vote for people who fund wards than for ones who praise the market.

say: I'd tell friends **nursing** is safe because machines can't do care, and the real problem is staffing.
I'd say we need to fund **wards** properly, not talk about software.
think: Privately, I'm worried about the **loan**, about thirty thousand by the end, and that Elmwood keeps cutting staff.
I'm sure I'll have a job, so my fear is **pay**, not machines.
do: Keep the **weekend shifts** at Elmwood and apply for the hospital bursary in second year.
Go to the student nurses' **union** meetings and stay away from AI tools.
feel: **Steady** about the work, but tight in the stomach about money.
S0.quote: Thirty thousand of loan is a number I do on the bus, and my mum's agency pay hasn't moved in four years.
fieldNote: She is calm about the job but carries real **debt** worries and a mother on flat pay.
Blames owners and government for staffing, not technology; a clear progressive voice.

steps.text: Keep working weekend shifts at Elmwood care home
Apply for the hospital bursary at the start of second year
Go to the student nurses' union branch meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit the offices before the wards. Booking, rotas and reports go to software, and care still needs hands. But I'd want rules so nobody uses it as an excuse to cut nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Elmwood would use it to cut hours. Fewer people in the office, then fewer on the floor, and the same managers saying it's progress. I'd feel it before I even qualify, because my Saturday shifts are the easiest to trim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for extra weekday shifts now while they still exist and save every pound I can. I'd learn the new charting system if the hospital makes me, but only then. And I'd push the union to ask for a say on any new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, mostly. It's slow and I see it coming, but I'm not someone who picks up new things quickly, and that makes me worry more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Elmwood would change first. What would you notice on an ordinary Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a Saturday the manager would read the rota off a screen instead of asking us. Last winter my manager texted me a shift change at midnight. If a program did that, nobody would even say sorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, Rosa, to keep her agency job and not sign anything new without asking me. She trusts whoever talks nicely to her, and I don't want her pushed into worse hours.

say: I'd say software takes **office work** first, and we need rules so nobody uses it to cut nurses.
I'd tell friends to join the **union** before changes arrive.
think: Privately, I think Elmwood will use it to cut **hours**, starting with my Saturday shifts.
I'm slow with new technology, and that makes me **nervous**, even though nursing should last.
do: Ask for extra **weekday** shifts now and save every pound before hours are trimmed.
Learn the hospital's charting system only when needed, and ask the union for a **say** on software.
feel: **Nervous**, because I see it coming but I'm slow to pick up new tools.
S1.quote: Last winter my manager texted me a shift change at midnight. If a program did that, nobody would even say sorry.
fieldNote: Her worry is concrete: the **Saturday** shifts that pay her bus fare are the easiest hours to cut.
Leans on the union rather than on learning tools; says her own slowness with technology adds to the fear.

steps.text: Ask Elmwood for extra weekday shifts while they last
Put aside part of each wage into a savings account
Push the student union to ask for a say on software
Wait to learn the hospital charting system until required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and governments aren't ready. People like my mum would get hurt first, and the companies would be the ones getting rich. We'd need protests, not just polite emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I wasted the degree. I'd finish about the time AI can do most thinking work, and robots would come for care about three years after. I'd keep telling people nursing is safe, but I wouldn't believe it every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree because I have no better plan, and I'd take every extra shift to build a cushion. I'd march with the union and write to my local MP. I wouldn't start learning AI tools out of panic; I'd rather learn the real hands-on skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit angry. Two years is nothing. My loan doesn't disappear if the job does, so I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the day after you heard it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take a leave from classes to work full time for a year if the hospitals froze hiring. The loan is for fees, but rent and the bus are mine. I'd sooner lose a year than sit in lectures and watch the money run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you most worry about at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Joao, he's fourteen. I'd tell him to learn a trade with his hands, since robots come later for those. And my mum, because her agency would replace carers first once robots can lift people.

say: I'd say it is **frightening** and governments are not ready; we need real protest, not polite emails.
I'd tell people nursing still matters, though I only half **believe** it.
think: Privately, I'd think I might have wasted my **degree**, since robots reach care about three years after.
My **loan** would stay even if the job vanished, so I'd do sums every night.
do: Take every extra **shift** to build a cushion and march with the union.
Consider pausing classes to work full time if hospitals freeze **hiring**, and write to my MP.
feel: **Scared** and angry, and a bit lost about whether the degree still counts.
S2.quote: My loan doesn't disappear if the job does, so I'd lie awake doing sums.
fieldNote: The **loan** and her mother's agency job drive the fear; she expects her own path to be at risk.
Her answer is organised and collective, not personal: union, protest and her MP.

steps.text: Take every extra shift available to build a cash cushion
March with the nurses' union and write to my MP
Consider pausing classes to work full time for a year
Warn mum Rosa not to sign new agency contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to finish the degree and see how the NHS and the care homes react. We'd have time to organise, which matters. But I'd still say governments always move last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be uneasy but not in a panic. I'd have two years of working as a registered nurse before robots get to the wards. That's a small window, and I'd want to use it to pay down some of the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the first two years while working weekends, and from third year I'd pick a placement where hands-on skills matter most, like elderly care. I'd try to get into the union's rep training. And I'd save a small monthly amount even if it's only twenty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the first one. I'd feel I can still do something. But I wouldn't say I feel safe, because I'd still be in the middle of the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years gives you a bit of space. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother, Joao, that he has time to pick a trade and I'd help with the homework tonight. For the loan, I'd want a plan from the university, because they should help students who might graduate into a changed world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different for your mum compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum could keep working until her agency fades out, and I'd help her get a place on a training course for something else. Five years is long enough to retrain my mum, if someone pays for it. She doesn't trust courses, but she'd trust me asking.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **organise**, but governments always move last.
I'd tell friends to pick **placements** where hands-on skills matter.
think: Privately, I'd feel **uneasy** but not panicked; I would get about two years as a nurse before robots reach wards.
I'd want to use that **window** to pay down some of the loan.
do: Save **twenty pounds** a month and pick elderly-care placements in third year.
Join the union's **rep training** and help my mum Rosa find a retraining course.
feel: Better than the fast one; I feel I can still **act**, but not safe.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to retrain my mum, if someone pays for it. She doesn't trust courses, but she'd trust me asking.
fieldNote: More controlled than the two-year case; she plans **placements** and small savings.
Her mother's retraining is as important to her as her own career, and she wants the university to help students.

steps.text: Save twenty pounds a month toward the student loan
Choose elderly-care placements in third year
Join the union's rep training course
Help my mum Rosa find a retraining course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it to build rules and safety nets. I'd still want the unions in the room, because companies won't plan for ordinary people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel almost fine. I'd qualify, work six or seven years as a nurse, maybe do a specialist course, and my loan would be shrinking before the robots arrive. It's the first picture where I could imagine a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned, finish the degree and work on the wards. People want a person there at the end, so I'd train in palliative care and pay the loan off early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. Not happy, because the world is still changing, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes in the way you think about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about children one day, and I'd want them to grow up where care is still done by people. If the system helps families through it, I'd feel hopeful. If not, I'd blame the people who got rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you even with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That companies won't use the ten years to prepare anyone. They'll wait until year nine and then say nobody told them. I'd worry about my mum's pension and about the care homes turning into machine warehouses.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and we must use it to build rules and safety nets.
I'd want **unions** in the room because companies won't plan for ordinary people.
think: Privately, I'd feel almost fine: I would **qualify**, work for years and shrink the loan first.
My worry is that companies wait until year nine, then say nobody **warned** them.
do: Finish the degree, work on the wards, then take a **specialist** course such as palliative care.
Start paying the **loan** early if I can.
feel: Fairly **calm**; I can breathe, though the world is still changing.
S4.quote: People want a person there at the end, so I'd train in palliative care and pay the loan off early.
fieldNote: The first scenario where she can picture a normal **life**; the long runway lets her plan.
Her remaining fear is about companies and her mother's **pension**, not her own job.

steps.text: Finish the nursing degree and work on a hospital ward
Train in palliative care after qualifying
Pay off the student loan early

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. My loan doesn't disappear if the job does, and I'd be graduating into the exact moment nobody knows what to do. What would help is a government that stops hospitals using software as a reason to cut staff, and a loan that shrinks if the job market breaks. And one thing you didn't ask: I'm the first in my family at university, so I feel I'm carrying my mum's hopes. A degree that keeps its value is not a luxury for me, it's the whole plan.

headlineQuote: A degree that keeps its value is not a luxury for me, it's the whole plan.
portrait: Grace is a **nursing** student from a city flat, working weekends in a care home to pay her bus fare.
A scholarship place and **top** results make her the first in her family at university, carrying her mum's hopes.
Progressive and union-minded, she blames **owners** and governments, not technology, and avoids AI tools entirely.
Calm in the slow scenarios, but in the fast ones the **loan** and her mother's agency job turn her alarmed.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture worries her most: she would graduate into confusion with the loan still due.
whatWouldHelp: A government that stops hospitals using software to cut **staff**, and a **loan** that shrinks if jobs vanish.
